summary: Adolf von Harnack (1851-1930 CE) was a German Lutheran church historian and theologian, the leading historian of dogma of his era and a central representative of liberal Protestant theology. His History of Dogma advanced the thesis that dogma is 'a work of the Greek spirit on the soil of the Gospel', and his Berlin lectures What Is Christianity? (Das Wesen des Christentums, 1900) gave liberal Protestantism one of its most widely read statements of the essence of Christianity.
description:
Adolf von Harnack was born in 1851 in Dorpat, Livonia (now Tartu, Estonia), then part of the Russian Empire, the son of the Lutheran theologian Theodosius Harnack. He studied at Dorpat and Leipzig, taught at Leipzig, Giessen, and Marburg, and in 1888 was called to the chair of church history at the University of Berlin, an appointment carried through by the Prussian state over the objections of church authorities uneasy at his critical treatment of dogma and of parts of the New Testament. He remained at Berlin until his retirement in 1921, and beyond his faculty work held major positions in German scholarly life: he directed the Royal Library in Berlin from 1905 and was the founding president of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society for the Advancement of Science from 1911. He was ennobled (the 'von') in 1914 and died in 1930.

Harnack's scholarly monument is the History of Dogma (Lehrbuch der Dogmengeschichte, 1886-1890), a critical history of Christian doctrine from its beginnings through the Reformation. Its governing thesis, read verbatim for this entry in the Buchanan translation, is that 'Dogma in its conception and development is a work of the Greek spirit on the soil of the Gospel': on his account the dogmatic structure of the church is not identical with the Gospel itself but is the product of its early encounter with Greek thought, so that the historian's task is to trace how dogma arose and thereby to distinguish the Gospel from its dogmatic forms. This 'hellenization' thesis is Harnack's position, stated here as his and widely contested since.

His most famous work, What Is Christianity? (Das Wesen des Christentums), consists of sixteen lectures delivered without notes at the University of Berlin in the winter term 1899-1900. Read verbatim for this entry: he proposes to answer the question 'solely in its historical sense', employing 'the methods of historical science, and the experience of life gained by studying the actual course of history'; he argues that 'either the Gospel is in all respects identical with its earliest form, in which case it came with its time and has departed with it; or else it contains something which, under differing historical forms, is of permanent validity', while cautioning against the critic who, like the child picking the leaves off a bulb to find its kernel, destroys the thing in analyzing it; and he summarizes the teaching of Jesus under three heads: 'Firstly, the kingdom of God and its coming. Secondly, God the Father and the infinite value of the human soul. Thirdly, the higher righteousness and the commandment of love.' In the same lectures he draws his much-debated christological conclusion, in the standard rendering, that the Gospel as Jesus proclaimed it has to do with the Father only and not with the Son; that formulation is reported here as the standard rendering across the scholarship, and the whole 'essence of Christianity' program is Harnack's attributed position.

Harnack's program met sharp rejection in the following generation, recorded here as the critics' attributed position: Karl Barth, who had studied under Harnack in Berlin, broke with the liberal theology Harnack represented, and in 1923 the two conducted a famous exchange of open letters in the journal Die Christliche Welt, Harnack defending a scientific theology grounded in historical investigation, Barth insisting that theology's ground is God's revelation. Confessional and dialectical theologians rejected Harnack's reduction of the Gospel to the fatherhood of God and the ethical kingdom as a modernizing distortion; his critics and his defenders alike, however, have treated his erudition as a historian of early Christianity as formidable. This entry attributes the hellenization thesis and the essence-of-Christianity program to Harnack, and the rejection of them to his critics, adjudicating neither.
editorial_notes:
Harnack is described here on the terms of his own program and of the historians who study him (neutrality #6). His two signature theses, that dogma is a Hellenization of the Gospel and that the permanent essence of Christianity is the kingdom of God, the fatherhood of God and the infinite value of the human soul, and the commandment of love, are stated strictly as HIS attributed positions (neutrality #1, #2); the confessional and Barthian rejection of that program is stated strictly as the critics' attributed position; the editor endorses neither.

CONFIDENCE HONESTY: two primary sources are rated high because they were read verbatim in open, public-domain full texts. (1) What Is Christianity? (Saunders translation, 1901) was read at the Internet Archive; verified word for word: the methodological statement ('It is solely in its historical sense that we shall try to answer this question here; that is to say, we shall employ the methods of historical science, and the experience of life gained by studying the actual course of history'), the kernel-and-husk argument ('either the Gospel is in all respects identical with its earliest form, in which case it came with its time and has departed with it; or else it contains something which, under differing historical forms, is of permanent validity', with the image of the child picking the leaves off a bulb), and the three heads ('Firstly, the kingdom of God and its coming. Secondly, God the Father and the infinite value of the human soul. Thirdly, the higher righteousness and the commandment of love.'). (2) The hellenization sentence of the History of Dogma, vol. 1 (Buchanan translation) was read at the Internet Archive and verified verbatim: 'Dogma in its conception and development is a work of the Greek spirit on the soil of the Gospel.' The famous sentence that the Gospel as Jesus proclaimed it 'has to do with the Father only and not with the Son' was NOT located verbatim in the portion of the open text consulted and is therefore reported only as the standard rendering across the scholarship, not personally verified; it is deliberately paraphrased with that flag in the description. The secondary studies (Glick, Rumscheidt, Welch) are rated medium: verified to exist and be on-topic via publisher, catalogue, and academic-review records (Glick reviewed in Church History and Religious Studies; Rumscheidt in the Scottish Journal of Theology monograph series, Cambridge University Press), not read line by line. Biographical details (Dorpat, the chairs, the 1888 Berlin appointment over church objections, the Royal Library, the Kaiser Wilhelm Society presidency, the 1914 ennoblement) rest on the secondary scholarship at medium; the dates 1851-1930 are secure and standardly reported.

Sourcing triangulates the three Christian lenses per neutrality #8: (a) academic studies of Harnack (Glick; Rumscheidt; Welch on the movement); (b) the primary corpus, Harnack's own What Is Christianity? and History of Dogma, both read in the open texts as described; (c) the contemporary theological reception through the Barth-Harnack correspondence of 1923 (Rumscheidt's edition and analysis), with Barth's side recorded as attributed critique. No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. This entry is referenced by liberal-theology (key_figure) and university-of-berlin (related_to).

lifespan.note: 1851-1930 CE; born in Dorpat, Livonia (now Tartu, Estonia); taught at Leipzig, Giessen, and Marburg, then at Berlin from 1888 to 1921; died in Heidelberg in 1930.

relations.note: A central representative of liberal Protestant theology, whose Berlin lectures What Is Christianity? (1900) gave the movement one of its most widely read statements; this entry supplies the key_figure referenced by liberal-theology.

Held the chair of church history at the University of Berlin from 1888 to 1921 and delivered there the lectures published as What Is Christianity? (Das Wesen des Christentums, 1900), whose title page attests they were 'delivered in the University of Berlin during the winter-term 1899-1900'.

Standardly placed by historians of doctrine in the school of Albrecht Ritschl (1822-1889), whose ethical, anti-metaphysical program Harnack developed in historical theology; recorded as the historians' standard placement.

Barth studied under Harnack in Berlin; Barth's later break with the liberal theology Harnack represented, and their 1923 exchange of open letters in Die Christliche Welt (Harnack defending scientific-historical theology, Barth insisting on revelation), is recorded as Barth's attributed critique, not adjudicated.

sources.citation: Harnack, Adolf von. What Is Christianity? (Das Wesen des Christentums, 1900). Sixteen lectures delivered in the University of Berlin during the winter-term 1899-1900. Translated by Thomas Bailey Saunders. London: Williams and Norgate; New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1901. Primary text, read in the open full text. Load-bearing passages verified verbatim: the historical method statement ('It is solely in its historical sense that we shall try to answer this question here; that is to say, we shall employ the methods of historical science, and the experience of life gained by studying the actual course of history'); the permanence argument ('either the Gospel is in all respects identical with its earliest form, in which case it came with its time and has departed with it; or else it contains something which, under differing historical forms, is of permanent validity'); and the three heads of the teaching of Jesus ('Firstly, the kingdom of God and its coming. Secondly, God the Father and the infinite value of the human soul. Thirdly, the higher righteousness and the commandment of love.').
